newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African analysts, press praise Manuel's budget.
newsitem.headline: S.African analysts, press praise Manuel's budget.

text.p: South African newspapers on Thursday resoundingly endorsed Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's first budget and analysts were uniformly impressed, leaving only the unions to carp at his proposals.
"Manuel silences market wolves," said Business Report.
"Government opts for fiscal rectitude," said Business Day.

Port Elizabeth's Eastern Province Herald noted the budget's endorsement of a macroeconomic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution (GEAR) released last June with its headline: "Shifting into GEAR."

Even the Afrikaans-language Burger, which seldom misses an opportunity to criticise President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC), said: "Budget puts emphasis in the right places."
Manuel, 16 days short of his first anniversary as finance minister, tabled a disciplined budget on Wednesday cutting state spending by a real 2.4 percent to 161.9 billion rand.
He delivered on the ANC's promise to cut the 1996/97 budget deficit to 5.1 percent of gross domestic product and estimated the deficit for the year to March 31, 1998, at 4.0 percent.
But for investors, Manuel's major news was his decision to dramatically relax the remaining foreign exchange controls inherited from apartheid rule, which ended in April 1994.

Manuel opened the way for individuals to invest abroad up to ceilings that would be decided before the concession takes effect in July, and either extended or expanded measures allowing institutions and corporates to buy beyond South Africa's borders.
The headlines from the markets showed steady rand gains against foreign currencies, with the rand-dollar price up almost four cents at 4.40 early on Thursday.
"Everyone says the budget is good, so let's sell dollars," said one senior trader, adding: "We will probably take it down to 4.38 and then people will say let's buy back dollars."
Bond yields continued to head lower as the market remained buoyant even after sleeping on Manuel's blueprint for poverty relief in an environment of tight fiscal discipline.
The key R150 government bond had a 14.615 percent yield early on Thursday compared with 14.74 percent when Manuel finished his speech on Wednesday.
Rand Merchant Bank chief economist Rudolf Gouws said Manuel had clearly put South Africa on the road to the growth, employment and redistribution as promised last June.
The GEAR programme links fiscal discipline, labour flexibility and export promotion to achieve massive job creation and growth of six percent by the turn of the century.

"He and his team were faced with numerous constraints, the biggest being the need to balance social demands with the fiscal commitments outlined in the government's macro-economic strategy," Gouws said.
"It is reassuring to see that Manuel resisted populist calls for increased government expenditure and, instead, has faced up to the hard fiscal realities."

The only concerted criticism came from the powerful Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), which, with the South African Communist Party, is part of the ANC's alliance that won power for Mandela in 1994.
Cosatu had called for an increase in the maximum tax rate from 45 percent to 55 percent to fund development and encouraged cautious borrowing to fire up the economy.
"It's a budget that in the main is put together to please international investors," Cosatu General Secretary Sam Shilowa said on Thursday.

But even Cosatu's criticism was muted. The federation welcomed Manuel's 2.8 billion rand in tax relief for people earning under 60,000 rand a year and his decision not to increase value added tax beyond the current 14 percent.
Business Report editor James Lamont declared the budget a vindication of Manuel's confidence in the face of cynicism about his lack of business education or experience.
"Manuel's polished performance and increasing mastery of his portfolio shows he has learned to tread the fiscal tightrope and win investor confidence.
"The political activist-cum-parliamentarian and now finance minister has come of age, and none to soon," Lamont said.
